title: The Lord Who Measured Zero
chapter: Chapter 2: The Mill That Wouldn't Turn

lines.text: Greyhollow, day one. Assets: one keep, half a roof, thirty-seven people, six goats, and a dog who now eats more than all of them combined.
Liabilities: four thousand crowns, owed to House Corrow, due at first thaw. Roughly ninety days.
I spent the morning walking the village with Bram. Nobody waved.
They've had four lords in ten years, my lord. They stopped learning the names.
The mill was the worst of it. A good stream, a good wheel, and both frozen solid.
Wheel's been dead three winters, my lord. Ice gets in the gears. We grind by hand now.
And you are?
Tobin. Blacksmith. Also miller, carpenter, and the man who fixes whatever the last lord broke.
I looked at the stream. Then at the hill above it. Then at the ditch someone had dug, badly, a long time ago.
The ice isn't the problem. Your water comes in too slowly. It pools behind the wheel and freezes before it can move.
And you know that how?
Chapter nine of On the Management of Northern Estates. Very dry. Excellent diagrams.
A book. He's going to fix the wheel with a book.
That was Wren. Village huntress, seventeen, and by the look of her, already certain I would fail.
We dug for four days. We re-cut the old channel, steeper and narrower, lined with stone, so the water would come in fast enough to stay alive.
Strange thing. Nobody got tired. Old men who had coughed all winter were swinging picks at dawn.
Good food and a clear goal. Morale is an underrated resource.
Morale. Right.
On the fifth morning, Tobin pulled the last stone out of the channel.
The water hit the wheel. The wheel groaned. And then it turned.
Ha! Three winters! Three winters, and it's turning!
The whole village was cheering. Even the goats looked impressed.
Fine. You're not useless. Yet.
Nobody noticed the frost on the mill roof melting. Not even me.
That afternoon, Wren went hunting. She told me later she drew her bow the same way she had a thousand times before.
The arrow flew two hundred paces. Then it went straight through a tree.
What.
That evening, Ash came home from the Pale with something in his mouth.
He dropped it at my feet. A blue crystal, glowing faintly, cold as winter.
Good boy. You brought me a rock.
My lord, that's not a rock. That's rimeglass. From a frost-wolf's heart.
One like that sells for forty crowns. Maybe fifty.
Forty crowns. I did the maths. Four thousand crowns is a hundred frost-wolves.
I looked at Ash. Ash looked at me. His tail thumped once.
We were going to need a bigger plan.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter three, coming soon.
